title: Why Python's self Is Explicit, Not Hidden (Borrowed From Modula-3)
explainer: Having to write `self` as an ordinary first parameter, rather than having it hidden the way C++'s and JavaScript's `this` are, was a deliberate design choice Python borrowed from the Modula-3 language. Python's own FAQ gives the rationale: it keeps instance attributes and methods visually distinguishable from local variables, and it makes calling an overridden base-class method (`BaseClass.method(self, ...)`) straightforward with no special operator needed. It's the reason the mutable-class-attribute bug in this lesson and the JS `this`-rebinding bug elsewhere in this track look so different — Python's object model just exposes plumbing other languages hide.

title: PEP 318 and the Arrival of @decorator Syntax (Python 2.4, 2004)
explainer: The `@trace` syntax shown in this lesson is younger than decorators themselves — `classmethod` and `staticmethod` already existed in Python 2.2, but applying them meant a clunky assignment written after the whole function body. PEP 318, debated on and off from 2002 through 2004, added the `@` syntax (deliberately styled after Java's annotations) that shipped in Python 2.4, turning the manual `add = trace(add)` rebinding into the one-line form used throughout this module.
